cells.tense: The endings arrive when they are due, and you trust what comes after them.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Some share has run out of proportion — time, effort, room in the week. Set it back to the honest measure once this week, then finish there. No follow-up.
cells.core:
You are in a stretch where things finish on their own schedule, and you let them go. What you are becoming shows in what you stop holding. That reads to the people nearby as calm — nothing being gripped past its day.

There's a share in your life that has run out of proportion. Maybe it's time, or effort, or room in a schedule that someone else keeps filling. This week, set it back to what's fair — one adjustment, plainly done — and then stop. Don't keep checking whether it took. Fairness flows when it's set and left; the re-checking is what makes it feel like a negotiation instead of a life. The ending you're in doesn't need managing. It needs one clean adjustment, and your hands off it after that.
cells.sheetLine: The endings arrive on time, and you let them.
cells.verb: ending what has finished, so what is next can begin

cells.tense: You will be braced for the next ending before this one has finished arriving.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Stay with a situation you are already inside — a stretch with someone, a change you began — through the uncomfortable part, rather than reaching for an exit.
cells.core:
You are ending things ahead of their time. Not because they're finished, but because the ending feels like relief, and relief is easier to reach for than the middle of something. Each fresh start looks like freedom from here. What's underneath is that nothing gets to live long enough to become what it was going to be.

There's a difference between ending what's done and leaving before it's done. This week, take something you're in the middle of and don't leave it. Stay in contact with it — the person, the situation, the change — through the part that's uncomfortable. You don't have to fix it or enjoy it. Just don't exit. Being reached by what's hard, without stepping away, tells you whether the thing was dying or whether you were. After that, decide with information instead of with the reflex.
cells.sheetLine: You end things early, and call the exit freedom.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that closed behind you, and still say you might go back through.
cells.act: move toward the thing you want, one step, today
cells.ask: A direction you want is already pulling at you. Take the smallest visible step toward it today, before you feel ready, and don't check whether the step was right.
cells.core:
You are holding onto something whose time has passed. It might be a role, a habit of loyalty, a version of a relationship that stopped being real. From inside, it reads as faithfulness — you are not the kind of person who walks away. But the walking away already happened, and you've been standing in the quiet since.

What you are is not going to come forward while you're guarding what's over. There's something you want that you haven't moved toward — a direction the feeling in you is already pulling. Today, take one step in that direction, however small, and don't wait to feel ready. You don't have to end the old thing with a speech or a ceremony. Moving toward what's alive is how the dead thing finishes itself. Take the step today, and nothing more is asked of you yet.

cells.tense: Something is finishing in you right now, and you have not named it as an ending.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: A change or loss is in motion with nowhere to sit. Give it a shape — a line written down, a slot on the calendar — so it stops leaking into everything else.
cells.core:
Something is ending in your life, and it hasn't been given a name. You feel the effects — a low hum, a restlessness, a sense that the ground has shifted slightly — but you've been treating it as a mood or a busy stretch. The ending is real. It just hasn't been put anywhere yet, so it's leaking into everything instead of sitting in one place.

The way through isn't insight first. It's structure. Take the thing in motion — the change, the loss, the finish — and give it a container. A line written down. A phrase that says where it sits. A place where it lives, so it stops living everywhere. You don't have to know what it means. You just have to make it carryable. Once it has a shape, you can pick it up and look at it. Until then, it's carrying you.

attempts.check: The cell for the Unacknowledged status risks claiming the person doesn't know what is ending in their life; the record supports 'operating without awareness' of something that is actually ending, not a blanket statement about their self-knowledge. A reader could reasonably say 'I know exactly what's ending, I just haven't acted on it' — so the ask should still work even if they already know. The ask survives being wrong: building a container for one ending works whether or not the person has named it, because the act is the structure, not the insight. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is any line implying the person is oblivious to their own life — the cell should render the mechanism as a part of life that hasn't been given a name, not as a person who never looks. The Too Much ask uses the partner act 'let yourself be reached by what they are carrying' but seat-specific phrasing must avoid implying the other person is required; the ask is one person's willingness, not a demand on anyone else.
